\chapter{Ten, Eleven, Twelve, and the au Sign}
\label{ch:mr-ten-to-twelve}
\hlchaptermodality{56}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count to twelve, hear the worn-down ten at the end of the teens, and write the au vowel sign.}

Complete MR-R56-ten-to-twelve and count to twelve, then name the worn-down dahaa hiding at the end of akraa and baaraa.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dahā]{\mr{दहा} (dahā) — ten}

\label{lesson:MR-C56-daha}



\begin{quote}
Count from \textbf{\mr{एक}} to \textbf{\mr{नऊ}} and stop. The book has taken you no further than that.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{दहा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{दहा}} — \emph{dahā} — \textbf{10}
\end{quote}

Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{दश}} (\emph{daśa}) — Latin \emph{decem}, English \textbf{ten}. This is the one to hold hardest, because the eleven-to-eighteen you are about to meet are all \emph{something-and-ten} with the ten worn down to a \textbf{-\mr{रा}} on the end.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dahā} — ten
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sahā sāt āṭh naū} — the run up to it, without looking
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hushār} — clever
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mī mhaṇto kī …} — I say that …
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is ten in Marathi? (\textbf{\mr{दहा}}.) Say the number before it, and the one before that.

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A6\%E0\%A4\%B9\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{दहा}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[akrā]{\mr{अकरा} (akrā) — eleven}

\label{lesson:MR-C56-akra}



\begin{quote}
Count from \textbf{\mr{एक}} to \textbf{\mr{दहा}} and stop. The book has taken you no further than that.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{अकरा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{अकरा}} — \emph{akrā} — \textbf{11}
\end{quote}

Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{एकादश}} (\emph{ekādaśa}), literally \emph{one-ten}. Say \textbf{\mr{अकरा}} slowly: the \textbf{\mr{अ}-} at the front is the \textbf{\mr{एक}} you have counted with since chapter thirteen, and the \textbf{-\mr{रा}} at the end is what is left of \textbf{\mr{दश}}.

That is the pattern for everything up to eighteen. Each one is a unit in front and a worn-down ten behind, and the \textbf{-\mr{रा}} is the tell.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{akrā} — eleven
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sāt āṭh naū dahā} — the run up to it, without looking
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{-ṇyāsāṭhī} — in order to
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is eleven in Marathi? (\textbf{\mr{अकरा}}.) Say the number before it, and the one before that.

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%85\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{अकरा}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bārā]{\mr{बारा} (bārā) — twelve}

\label{lesson:MR-C56-bara}



\begin{quote}
Count from \textbf{\mr{एक}} to \textbf{\mr{अकरा}} and stop. The book has taken you no further than that.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{बारा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{बारा}} — \emph{bārā} — \textbf{12}
\end{quote}

Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{द्वादश}} (\emph{dvādaśa}), \emph{two-ten}. The \textbf{\mr{द्वा}-} flattened to \textbf{\mr{बा}-} and the \textbf{-\mr{दश}} to \textbf{-\mr{रा}}, and the second half is identical to the second half of \textbf{\mr{अकरा}}. One pattern, twice.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bārā} — twelve
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{āṭh naū dahā akrā} — the run up to it, without looking
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sopī} — easy
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is twelve in Marathi? (\textbf{\mr{बारा}}.) Say the number before it, and the one before that.

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AC\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{बारा}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-au]{\mr{ौ} — the au vowel sign}

\label{lesson:MR-W56-au-matra}



\begin{quote}
You can write every number so far. The next one but one needs a vowel sign the book has never taught.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ौ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ौ}} is \emph{au}, and it is the \textbf{\mr{ो}} you have had since chapter one with a second stroke added. That is the whole relationship: \textbf{\mr{ो}} is \emph{o}, \textbf{\mr{ौ}} is \emph{au}, and the extra mark is the difference — exactly as \textbf{\mr{े}} and \textbf{\mr{ै}} will pair in a later chapter.

Say the two apart before you write them. \textbf{\mr{को}} is \emph{ko}; \textbf{\mr{कौ}} is \emph{kau}, a fuller sound with the mouth opening wider.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{कौ}} twice with the model visible. Then write \textbf{\mr{को}} beside it and check that only one of the two carries the second stroke.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \textbf{\mr{ो}} and \textbf{\mr{ौ}} has two strokes? (\textbf{\mr{ौ}}.) What is the number it was taught for? (\textbf{Fourteen}, next chapter.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A5\%8C}{Devanagari au vowel sign}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dahā · akrā · bārā]{Ten, and the first two of the -\mr{रा} family built on it}

\label{lesson:MR-R56-ten-to-twelve}



\begin{quote}
Count from \textbf{\mr{एक}} to \textbf{\mr{बारा}}. Then say only the two that end in \textbf{-\mr{रा}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ek} … \emph{bārā} — the whole run
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{akrā}, \emph{bārā} — and hear the same \textbf{-\mr{रा}} twice
  \item \emph{Say it:} what that \textbf{-\mr{रा}} used to be — \emph{\textbf{\mr{दश}}}, the Sanskrit ten
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{uṁch} — tall
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{-lyāvar} — after doing
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is hiding at the end of \textbf{\mr{अकरा}} and \textbf{\mr{बारा}}? (\textbf{The word for ten}.) How far can you count? (\textbf{To twelve}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
